newsitem.title: CHINA: China says surviving Gang of Four member freed.
newsitem.headline: China says surviving Gang of Four member freed.

text.p: China said on Monday that the sole surviving member of the notorious Gang of Four that was led by Jiang Qing, wife of Chairman Mao Zedong, had been freed after serving a 20-year term for subversive crimes.
"Yao Wenyuan was released upon completion of his sentence on October 5," a spokesman for the State Council, or cabinet, said in the first official word on him for many years.
"The relevant departments have already made appropriate arrangements for him," the spokesman said by telephone.

Yao, 64, was arrested on October 6, 1976, along with the three other members of the Gang of Four, when one of the most sensational moments in the power struggles in China's Communist Party ended a decade of ultra-leftist fervour whipped up by Mao's wife.

Chinese sources said Yao has been out of prison since 1994, living under medical parole in utmost secrecy in his hometown of Shanghai. He received the most lenient sentence of the four -- 20 years for counter-revolutionary, or subversive, crimes.
The State Council official refused to give Yao's current whereabouts.

He said the former member of the powerful party Politburo -- a heavily-built, round-faced and balding man when he was last seen in public at his 1980-81 trial -- was deprived of his political rights for the next five years. That means he cannot meet foreign reporters or publish articles.
Yao can expect to spend the remaining years of his life under tight surveillance and in deep obscurity.

Chinese official media have kept silent on the 20th anniversary of the arrest of the Gang of Four by the chief of Mao's palace security staff, just one month after the death of the Great Helmsman removed their main support.
The issue of their guilt and close links to Mao -- who is still officially revered -- is one that embarrasses communist officialdom and is relegated to the darkest of corners.

Jiang Qing, leader of the Gang of Four that wielded supreme power during the Cultural Revolution, was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve in 1981 for the deaths of tens of thousands in the Cultural Revolution. She never repented but her sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
The former Shanghai starlet, dubbed a witch by state media after her downfall, hanged herself in Beijing in May 1991.
Zhang Chunqiao received a suspended death sentence after refusing to utter a single word during the two-month trial. He died in 1991, according to the Encyclopedia of the People's Republic of China.
The fourth and youngest gang member, Wang Hongwen, died of liver cancer in a Beijing hospital in 1992 while serving a life sentence.

Yao has been spending his days wielding the pen that wrote his rise to power. He has been writing a book and studying Chinese history since his release on medical parole two years ago, Chinese sources said.
